title: The introduction calls the fragmentation index the cost of an *optimal* foresight plan; Section 4.2 says the same plan is not optimal even with foresight
where_a: 1_introduction.tex:96 — "We formalize this idea in a \emph{fragmentation index}, the expected cost of an optimal execution plan with foresight into AI's successes and failures, and show analytically that it approximately tracks the impact of optimal AI deployment."
where_b: 4_implications.tex:202 — "Notably, this AI strategy isn't necessarily optimal even with the benefit of foresight: a long AI chain with a good probability of success might be optimal even if the prophet knows that it will fail on the first attempt."
why: The fragmentation index is defined (4_implications.tex:198-214) as the expected cost of one specific prophet strategy: chain every maximal run of steps that will succeed, execute the rest individually. Section 4.2 explicitly states that this strategy is not the optimal plan under foresight, and that is precisely why Proposition 2 has to prove a constant-factor approximation (1/8 or 1/4 to 5/4) rather than an equality. If FI were "the expected cost of an optimal execution plan with foresight" the two-sided bounds and Example OA-2 (A_omitted_proofs.tex:240-246, FI/OPT = 5/4) would be describing something else. The introduction also repeats the claim at line 101 ("Our fragmentation index is the closed-form counterpart of that program").
fix: The introduction is wrong. Replace "an optimal execution plan with foresight" with a neutral description of the actual object, e.g. "a simple execution plan built with foresight into AI's successes and failures, which chains together the steps that will succeed."

title: Prose says the prophet performs all failed steps manually; the formula it introduces charges them the cheaper of manual and augmented
where_a: 4_implications.tex:200 — "The prophet might therefore chain together all contiguous sequences of tasks that would all succeed, and perform all other tasks manually."
where_b: 4_implications.tex:212 — realized fragmentation is "$\sum_{i \in F}\min\left\{\manualTime{i}, \frac{\AItime{i}}{q_i}\right\} + \sum_{C_j \in \mathcal{C}} \omega(C_j)$"; and A_omitted_proofs.tex:196 — "$\minTime{i}$ is the minimum cost to implement step $s_i$ individually (whether manually or through AI augmentation)."
why: The prose describes the prophet's strategy as executing every non-succeeding step manually, at cost $\manualTime{i}$. The formula it is introducing charges each failed step $\min\{\manualTime{i}, \AItime{i}/q_i\}$, i.e. it may execute the step as a standalone augmented step instead. These differ whenever $\AItime{i}/q_i < \manualTime{i}$, which is exactly the AI-easy case that the surrounding examples turn on (Example 1's easy step: $\AItime{2}/q_2 \approx 4.44 < \manualTime{2} = 8$). The appendix restatement of the same construction is careful about this (A_omitted_proofs.tex:195-198); the main-text prose is not.
fix: The prose is wrong. Change "and perform all other tasks manually" to "and execute every other step on its own, manually or as a standalone augmented step, whichever is cheaper." The same slip recurs at 4_implications.tex:232 ("with chains of length 1 converted to manual execution when appropriate"), which the appendix (A_omitted_proofs.tex:261) states correctly as "either manually or augmented, whichever is cheaper."

title: Appendix B gives Job 1 the skill of step 2, which is an automated step the model says requires no skill
where_a: B_macro_production.tex:26 — "The worker assigned to perform Job 1 is required to obtain not only the skill required for manual Task 1, $\manualSkill{1}$, but must also possess the required skill for AI-assisted Task 2, $\AIskill{2}$ ... and equals $\manualSkill{1} + \AIskill{2}$."
where_b: 5_longrun.tex:40 — "An AI chain therefore demands only the skill required to check and validate the output of its augmented step, and an automated step inside a chain demands no skill of anyone, since no human ever handles it directly"; 5_longrun.tex:122 — "$\skillcost{b}$ & Skill required by task $b$: $\manualSkill{i}$ if a manual step, $\AIskill{r}$ if an AI chain augmented at step $r$; an automated step requires none"
why: Appendix B's example is Job 1 of Figure 4 (fig:hierarchical_production). In that figure (plots/TikZ_visualization/hierarchical_production_illustration.tex, lines 18-24 and 45) Task 2 is the AI chain over Steps 2-4, with Steps 2 and 3 automated and Step 4 augmented; 3_shortrun.tex:24 states the same ("here steps 2--4 become Task~2"). By the rule in 5_longrun.tex:122 the skill of Task 2 is $\AIskill{4}$, the skill of managing the augmented endpoint. $\AIskill{2}$ is the skill of managing an AI attempt at step 2, which is automated and by the model's own statement demands no skill of anyone. The error is a task index used where a step index is required; it propagates to \eqref{eq:new_wage} (B_macro_production.tex:33), which sums $\manualSkill{b}$ and $\AIskill{b}$ over task indices $b$, and to $\alpha^{-d_b}$ at B_macro_production.tex:48 and :80, where $d$ is defined as a step-level difficulty (3_shortrun.tex:113). 3_shortrun.tex:124 states the convention that is being broken: "Step-level primitives are indexed by $i$ and task-level objects by $b$."
fix: Appendix B is wrong. Write Job 1's wage as $\manualSkill{1} + \AIskill{4}$, and in \eqref{eq:new_wage} and the skill-adjusted-time definition replace the step-level primitives carrying task indices with the task-level skill $\skillcost{b}$ (or write $\AIskill{r(b)}$ for the augmented endpoint $r(b)$ of chain $b$, and $d(T_b)=\sum_{i\in T_b}d_i$ for the chain difficulty).

title: "AI-exposed" means E1-only and E1-or-E2 in the same regression discussion
where_a: 7_empirics.tex:99 — "\emph{$\text{ai\_exposure}_{o}$} is the share of AI-exposed tasks ... We additionally control for \emph{$\text{num\_ai\_able\_steps}_{o}$}, the number of AI-exposed (E1- or E2-labeled) steps in the occupation"; and 7_empirics.tex:116 — "We count as AI-exposed both E1- and E2-exposed tasks, which together account for 44\% of the tasks in the dataset."
where_b: 7_empirics.tex:132 (table notes) — "The variable ``AI Exposure'' denotes the share of AI-exposed (E1) steps in the occupation"; identically at D_tables_and_robustness.tex:99; and C_sample_construction.tex:16 — "we treat tasks with a human-assigned E1 label as exposed to AI and those with E0 or E2 labels as unexposed to AI."
why: The single term "AI-exposed" is given two incompatible extensions inside one subsection: the E1+E2 set (44% of tasks, used for the EFI and for the count control) and the E1-only set (14% of tasks per the footnote at line 116, used for the regressor plotted in the tables). A reader cannot tell from the text which set \text{ai\_exposure} is built from, since line 99 defines it as "the share of AI-exposed tasks" immediately before a sentence that uses "AI-exposed" to mean E1-or-E2, while the table note says E1.
fix: Both sides are defensible as constructions; the terminology is not. Reserve "AI-exposed" for the E1-only default declared in C_sample_construction.tex:16 and use a distinct label (e.g. "AI-able" or "E1/E2-exposed") everywhere the E1+E2 set is meant, including line 116, the num_ai_able_steps control, and the EFI definition; then make line 99 state which of the two \text{ai\_exposure} uses.

title: The empirical fragmentation index is described as "the number of AI blocks per step", contradicting its own definition three paragraphs later
where_a: 7_empirics.tex:99 — "Because the fragmentation index is the number of AI blocks per step, it varies mechanically with how many AI-able steps a workflow contains"
where_b: 7_empirics.tex:108-112 — "the empirical fragmentation index is the ratio of the number of \emph{potential} tasks in the sense of our theoretical framework to the total number of steps ... If none of the five tasks are exposed to AI, then the number of tasks in the theoretical sense is five, and the EFI equals $5/5 = 1$."
why: The two characterizations give different numbers on the paper's own example. Under the definition, an occupation with five steps and none exposed has EFI $=5/5=1$; under "number of AI blocks per step" it would be $0/5=0$. With two consecutive exposed steps the definition gives $4/5=0.8$ (three manual tasks plus one AI block), whereas "AI blocks per step" gives $1/5=0.2$. The numerator of EFI counts all potential tasks, manual steps included, not just AI blocks. "AI block" is also an undefined synonym for "AI chain" here and at 2_literature.tex:28.
fix: Line 99 is wrong. Replace with "Because the index counts potential tasks per step, it falls mechanically as a workflow contains more AI-able steps" and use "AI chain" rather than "AI block".

title: Section 4.2 and the proofs call steps "tasks" in the very sentences that define step-level failure, contradicting Section 3's primitive/designated distinction
where_a: 4_implications.tex:205 — "suppose that each step $s_i$ succeeds independently with probability $q_i$; any task that does not succeed is said to fail"
where_b: A_omitted_proofs.tex:190 (the appendix restatement of the identical sentence) — "Suppose that each step $s_i$ succeeds independently with probability $q_i$; any step that does not succeed is said to fail."
why: Section 3 makes "step" the primitive and "task" a contiguous block the firm designates (3_shortrun.tex:34, :62, :93), and 3_shortrun.tex:124 fixes the index convention. Success probabilities $q_i$ attach to steps, not to tasks; the appendix version of the sentence says "step" where the body says "task", so the two statements of the same definition disagree. The same substitution recurs throughout the passage and the proofs: 4_implications.tex:198 ("which tasks would be completed successfully by AI on its first attempt"), :200 ("contiguous sequences of tasks"), :232 ("The algorithm groups tasks into chains" — chains are groups of steps, and a chain *is* a task), :246 ("the probability that a task of normalized difficulty $1$ is completed successfully" — $d_i$ is a step primitive), A_omitted_proofs.tex:185, :219-221 ("each failed task $s_i \in T_j$", where $T_j$ is the task and $s_i$ the step), :281 ("the final task $s_m$"), :300, :358.
fix: The body and proof prose are wrong; the appendix's line 190 wording is the correct one. Replace "task" with "step" wherever the object carries a step index $s_i$/$i$ or a success probability $q_i$ or difficulty $d_i$, and keep "task" only for elements of $\T$.

title: The short-run DP proof says "task $k$ cannot be automated ... it can only be augmented or performed manually", applying step-level execution modes to a task
where_a: A_omitted_proofs.tex:454 — "because of the way we defined $C[k]$, task $k$ cannot be automated in any minimum-cost solution that determines $C[k]$; it can only be augmented or performed manually"; and :467 — "we then separately optimize the production strategy for tasks $1$ through $\ell$"
where_b: 3_shortrun.tex:45-91 — manual, augmented and automated are defined as modes of a *step* ("A step $i$ is performed manually...", "A step $i$ is augmented...", "A step is automated..."), and 3_shortrun.tex:93 defines a task as "either a manual step or an AI chain"
why: $C[k]$ is defined over steps 1 through $k$ (A_omitted_proofs.tex:453, and the recursion at :460-462 indexes $\manualTime{k}$, $\AItime{k}$, $q_i$, all step primitives), and $\ell$ is a step index. The claim being made is about step $k$ and steps $1..\ell$. A task has no automated/augmented/manual mode in the model: those are step modes, and a task is either a manual step or an AI chain. As written, the sentence asserts something the model's definitions do not permit.
fix: The proof is wrong. Write "step $k$ cannot be automated ... it can only be augmented or performed manually" and "optimize the production strategy for steps $1$ through $\ell$."

title: "Workflow-level AI exposure" is defined as realized AI deployment, the opposite of the exposure/execution distinction the empirics rest on
where_a: 4_implications.tex:135 — "we can interpret workflow-level AI exposure as the extent to which an optimal AI strategy employs AI automation and augmentation" (subsection title, line 130: "Workflow-level AI Exposure and the Fragmentation Index")
where_b: 7_empirics.tex:8 — the dataset records "its AI exposure status (exposed or unexposed to AI), which we interpret as the difficulty of the step for AI, its realized mode of execution (manual, AI-augmented, or AI-automated)", and \eqref{eq:fragmentation_index_regression} regresses ai_execution on ai_exposure as two distinct objects
why: Section 4.2 defines workflow-level "AI exposure" as an outcome (how much AI the optimal strategy actually uses), which is Section 7's ai_execution, not its ai_exposure. Section 7's whole Prediction 2 is that exposure does not translate one-for-one into execution, which is unstatable if exposure just means realized deployment. Section 4.2 itself uses the ex-ante sense three lines later: "a workflow ... is less exposed to large-scale automation, even though its step-level exposure to AI may appear high" (4_implications.tex:138), where the second "exposure" is amenability, not deployment.
fix: Section 4.2 is the loose side. Reserve "exposure" for ex-ante amenability throughout (matching Section 7 and Section 2's usage at 2_literature.tex:16-20) and rename the line-135 object, e.g. "the extent of AI deployment in a workflow"; adjust the subsection title accordingly.

title: Hand-off cost is defined on steps but the specialization example indexes it by task
where_a: 5_longrun.tex:90-91 — "given step $s_i$, we write $\handofftime{i}$ for the additional hand-off time spent by a worker for whom the last step of their job is $s_i$ ... The final job hands off to no one, so $\handofftime{m} = 0$"; Table 3 (5_longrun.tex:127) — "$\handofftime{i}$ & Hand-off time incurred when a worker's final step is $s_i$"
where_b: 5_longrun.tex:199 — "$\bigl(\skillcost{b},\, \timecost{b},\, \handofftime{b}\bigr)_{b=1,2,3} = (3,\,1,\,3),\quad (1,\,2,\,0.5),\quad (2,\,2,\,0)$"; and :205 — "the large hand-off time $\handofftime{1}=3$ that a boundary between tasks 1 and 2 would trigger"
why: 5_longrun.tex:87 makes the step-attachment the substantive point of the whole construction ("We therefore attach the hand-off cost to the step at which the break occurs rather than to the worker or to the number of jobs"), and 3_shortrun.tex:124 fixes $i$ for step-level primitives and $b$ for task-level objects. The example then supplies $\handofftime{b}$ per task, so $\handofftime{1}$ denotes the hand-off after task 1 rather than after step 1. Since a task can span several steps, the two indices are not interchangeable.
fix: The example is the loose side. Either write the hand-off as $\handofftime{}(T_b)$, defined as $\handofftime{i}$ for the final step $i$ of task $b$, or state explicitly that in this example each task is a single step so the indices coincide.

title: The introduction names the AI chain a "meta-task"; the model names it a "composite task"
where_a: 1_introduction.tex:11 — "some steps are chained together and automated, creating a meta-task whose output is validated by a human worker"; and :50 — "putting certain production steps ``under the hood'' of a logical meta-task"
where_b: 3_shortrun.tex:68 — "The AI chain as a whole can be thought as a single \emph{composite} task delegated by the human to AI for execution"; and 7_empirics.tex:22 — "forming a composite task per our model's definition"
why: The same object gets two names and neither passage acknowledges the other. "Meta-task" appears only in the introduction and is never defined or used again; "composite task" is the term the model and the empirical section use. The introduction also introduces the object a third way at line 15 ("lumping them together into one logical task").
fix: The introduction is the outlier. Use "composite task" in both introduction passages, or drop the second name and rely on "AI chain" throughout.

title: The same steps are called AI-easy, AI-able and AI-friendly within one example
where_a: 4_implications.tex:143 — "steps $1$ and $3$ are AI-easy and steps $2$ and $4$ are AI-hard"; figure caption 4_implications.tex:146 — "Dispersed AI-Able Steps"; figure notes :153 — "no two AI-able steps are ever adjacent"
where_b: 4_implications.tex:158 (the body sentence restating the same figure note) — "Because every easy step is flanked by hard ones, no two AI-friendly steps are ever adjacent"
why: Example 1 (4_implications.tex:56-58) introduces "AI-easy" and "AI-hard" as the paper's named step types, and Examples 2-3 are built from those exact parameter bundles. Within a single example the same two steps are then labelled AI-easy, AI-able and AI-friendly, and the figure note and body sentence differ only in that word. "AI-suitable" is a fourth variant for the same idea (4_implications.tex:3, :100; 2_literature.tex:19), and "automatable" a fifth (4_implications.tex:216, A_omitted_proofs.tex:185), which is doubly loose since automation in the model requires membership in a multi-step chain.
fix: Pick one term. "AI-easy/AI-hard" is the only pair the paper actually defines, so use it for the step types and drop "AI-able", "AI-friendly", "AI-suitable" and "automatable" from the theory sections (the empirical sections may keep "AI-able" if it is defined there as the E1/E2 set).

title: Three different things are each called "the smallest unit of work"
where_a: 3_shortrun.tex:34 — "Steps are the smallest unit of work in our framework."
where_b: B_macro_production.tex:40 — "Next, we define skill-adjusted labor, which is the smallest unit of work in our analysis." (3_shortrun.tex:62 adds a third: "Tasks are the smallest unit of work for a human worker.")
why: "In our framework" and "in our analysis" are the same scope, so two different objects are being given the same superlative. The task claim at 3_shortrun.tex:62 is at least qualified ("for a human worker"), but skill-adjusted labor is a derived quantity of tasks (B_macro_production.tex:44), so it cannot be smaller than a step.
fix: Appendix B is the loose side. Say skill-adjusted labor is "the unit of labor input in the aggregation" rather than "the smallest unit of work".

title: Appendix C equates occupation with job; Section 7 equates occupation with workflow, and the model makes a workflow contain several jobs
where_a: C_sample_construction.tex:11 — "In what follows, we use the terms step, task, and O*NET task interchangeably, as in the main text; likewise, we use job and occupation interchangeably."
where_b: 7_empirics.tex:19 and :24 — "each occupation's workflow corresponds to the model's step sequence" ... "We similarly use the terms workflow and occupation interchangeably without restating the mapping each time"
why: In the model a job is one worker's contiguous block of tasks and a workflow generally contains several of them: Figure 4 has $m=7$ steps, $n=5$ tasks and $p=3$ jobs (5_longrun.tex:25-26). Identifying occupation with workflow and occupation with job therefore identifies workflow with job, which the long run explicitly denies. Section 7 never uses "job" for an occupation, so Appendix C's declaration is unsupported by the usage it claims to follow ("as in the main text").
fix: Appendix C is the outlier. Change its declaration to "we use workflow and occupation interchangeably", matching 7_empirics.tex:24.

title: "Time and skill content of individual tasks" and "chaining together easy tasks" describe step-level primitives as task-level
where_a: 6_extensions.tex:95 — "Paired with detailed measurement of the time and skill content of individual tasks, the algorithms above could be run on real workflows"; 1_introduction.tex:101 — "both the exact and the approximate plan drive down costs by chaining together easy tasks"
where_b: 3_shortrun.tex:110-114 and 5_longrun.tex:120-121 — the measured primitives are step-level: "$\manualTime{i}$ Time cost of completing step $i$ manually", "$d_i$ Difficulty of step $i$ for AI", "$\manualSkill{i}$ Skill required to complete step $i$ manually"; and 3_shortrun.tex:89 — an AI chain is "a contiguous block of one or more sequential steps"
why: The dynamic programs of Section 6.2 take step-level $(\manualSkill{i},\manualTime{i},\AIskill{i},\AItime{i},q_i,\handofftime{i})$ as inputs and produce tasks as output, so the measurement the paragraph calls for is of steps, not tasks. Likewise chains are formed from steps; "chaining together easy tasks" inverts the construction, since the chain is itself the task.
fix: Both are the loose side: write "the time and skill content of individual steps" and "chaining together easy steps". The same substitution is needed at 2_literature.tex:5 ("the ordering of tasks in production") and :27 ("when tasks are complementary because of sequencing"), both of which describe this paper's own mechanism.

title: Automation is said to be unavailable because no chain forms, although the paper's convention makes every augmented step a chain
where_a: 4_implications.tex:158 — "no two AI-friendly steps are ever adjacent, so no chain longer than a single step can form, and automation, which executes a step for free but is available only inside a chain, never becomes an option"
where_b: 3_shortrun.tex:76-77 — "an AI chain may consist of a single step, with $\ell = r$: having no automated predecessors, it is simply an augmented step. An AI-augmented step is thus an AI chain of length one, a convention we adopt throughout the paper."
why: Under the stated convention every augmented step is a chain, so "available only inside a chain" is satisfied by the two augmented steps in this example and does not by itself rule automation out. The condition that actually rules it out is chain length at least two, which Definition 4 supplies ("all steps but the final one are automated"). As written the sentence's stated reason does not support its conclusion given the paper's own convention.
fix: The sentence in Section 4.2 is the loose side: "automation, which executes a step for free but requires a chain of at least two steps, never becomes an option."

title: Lemma A.3 asserts the marginal-benefit function "jumps upward" at reorganization thresholds, but its proof derives only a weak inequality, which permits no jump at all and hence no non-monotonicity
where_a: A_omitted_proofs.tex:405 (Lemma \ref{lem:reorg_threshold}): "Moreover, at every reorganization threshold (where the optimal AI strategy changes), $g^*$ jumps upward." — and 4_implications.tex:250: "the marginal return to AI quality jumps up discontinuously"; 4_implications.tex:253: "at each threshold the returns jump upward"
where_b: A_omitted_proofs.tex:437-444: "A differentiable function with such a sign change has nonpositive derivative in the local neighborhood of $\alpha_0$. So $\phi'(\alpha_0) \le 0$, or equivalently, $C_{\T'}'(\alpha_0) \le C_\T'(\alpha_0)$" ... "$g_\T(\alpha_0) = -C_\T'(\alpha_0) \le -C_{\T'}'(\alpha_0) = g_{\T'}(\alpha_0)$"
why: The chain of inequalities in the proof is weak throughout: from $\phi(\alpha_0^-)\ge 0$, $\phi(\alpha_0)=0$, $\phi(\alpha_0^+)\le 0$ one gets only $\phi'(\alpha_0)\le 0$, hence $g_\T(\alpha_0)\le g_{\T'}(\alpha_0)$. Equality is not excluded: if $\phi$ has a triple root at $\alpha_0$ (e.g. $\phi(\alpha)=-c(\alpha-\alpha_0)^3$, which is compatible with the sign pattern and with $\phi$ being a difference of finite sums of powers of $\alpha$), then $\phi'(\alpha_0)=0$ and $g^*$ is continuous at the threshold. In that case $g^*$ is non-increasing on each regime and continuous across the threshold, i.e. globally non-increasing, which is exactly the opposite of the non-monotonicity the body advertises. The proof therefore establishes "$g^*$ does not jump downward," not "$g^*$ jumps upward." Separately, the intermediate sentence at line 437 is false as written: a sign change at $\alpha_0$ gives $\phi'\le 0$ at the point $\alpha_0$, not "in the local neighborhood."
fix: The proof side is what is wrong. Either weaken the lemma and the body prose to "$g^*$ does not fall at a reorganization threshold (and rises strictly whenever $\phi'(\alpha_0)\neq 0$)," or add a hypothesis ruling out tangential crossings (e.g. $\phi'(\alpha_0)\neq 0$, i.e. the two strategy-cost curves cross transversally) and state that hypothesis in the lemma. Also replace "nonpositive derivative in the local neighborhood of $\alpha_0$" with "nonpositive derivative at $\alpha_0$."

title: Proposition 4's hypothesis that all hand-off costs lie in $[1/B,B]$ is violated by every workflow in the model, since the model fixes the last step's hand-off cost at zero — and the proof itself relies on that zero
where_a: 6_extensions.tex:90 (Proposition \ref{prop:totalcost_optimization_dp}): "Fix a workflow with $m$ steps whose skill, time, and hand-off costs lie in $[1/B, B]$ for some $B > 0$." Repeated verbatim at A_omitted_proofs.tex:538: "Suppose all skill, time, and hand-off costs lie in $[1/B, B]$ for some $B > 0$."
where_b: 5_longrun.tex:91: "The final job hands off to no one, so $\handofftime{m} = 0$." And the proof relies on it: A_omitted_proofs.tex:493: "Note then that $V(m)$ is the solution to the desired optimization problem, recalling that the hand-off time for the final job will always be $0$."
why: $[1/B,B]$ with $B>0$ forces every hand-off cost to be at least $1/B>0$, so $\handofftime{m}=0$ is excluded. But $\handofftime{m}=0$ is imposed by the model as a primitive (5_longrun.tex:91), is used in the worked example of Section 5.3 ($\handofftime{3}=0$ at 5_longrun.tex:199 and in tables/job_design_example_with_handoff.tex), and is invoked inside the very proof of Proposition 4 to justify $V(m)=W(m,0,0)$. The hypothesis as stated is therefore satisfied by no instance of the model. The proof is half aware of this: A_omitted_proofs.tex:540 says "every non-zero skill or time cost is at least $1/B$," implicitly conceding that zero costs occur.
fix: The hypothesis is the wrong side. State it as "every non-zero skill, time, and hand-off cost lies in $[1/B,B]$" (or explicitly exempt $\handofftime{m}=0$) in both 6_extensions.tex:90 and A_omitted_proofs.tex:538. Nothing in the complexity accounting changes, since the bounds $[1/B,mB]$ and $[1/B,2mB^3]$ are already derived from the non-zero costs.

title: The prophet story used to motivate the fragmentation index says failed steps are done manually, but the formal definition of realized fragmentation prices them at the cheaper of manual and standalone augmentation
where_a: 4_implications.tex:200-201: "The prophet might therefore chain together all contiguous sequences of tasks that would all succeed, and perform all other tasks manually. The fragmentation index is then the expected cost of this strategy, under the assumption that the prophet's foresight is correct."
where_b: 4_implications.tex:\eqref{eq:fragmentation} (lines 214-217): "$\sum_{i \in F}\min\left\{\manualTime{i}, \frac{\AItime{i}}{q_i}\right\} + \sum_{C_j \in \mathcal{C}} \omega(C_j)$", repeated in A_omitted_proofs.tex:263 as "$\sum_{s_i \in F}\minTime{i} + \sum_{C_j \in \mathcal{C}} \omega(C_j)$" with A_omitted_proofs.tex:261 defining "$\minTime{i} = \min\{\manualTime{i}, \AItime{i}/q_i\}$ ... the minimum cost to implement step $s_i$ individually (whether manually or through AI augmentation)"
why: The two prescriptions differ whenever $\AItime{i}/q_i < \manualTime{i}$, which is exactly the paper's own "AI-easy" step: with $(\manualTime{},\AItime{},q)=(8,4,0.9)$ from Example \ref{ex:ca_predecessor}, a failed step contributes $\min\{8,4.44\}=4.44$ under the formula but $8$ under "perform all other tasks manually." The same mismatch appears on the other term: $\omega(C_j)=\min\{1,\sum_{i\in C_j}\manualTime{i}\}$ lets a successful run be priced manually rather than chained, contrary to "chain together all contiguous sequences of tasks that would all succeed." Formula and prose cannot both describe the same strategy.
fix: The prose is the loose side (the formula is what both Lemma \ref{lem:FI.upper.bound} and Lemma \ref{lem:FI.lower.bound.4} actually use). Rewrite 4_implications.tex:200 as "...and executes every other step on its own in whichever mode is cheaper, manual or augmented" and add that a successful run is chained only when that beats doing it manually.

title: The introduction calls the fragmentation index the cost of an optimal foresight plan; Section 4.2 states the same plan is not optimal even with foresight
where_a: 1_introduction.tex:96: "We formalize this idea in a \emph{fragmentation index}, the expected cost of an optimal execution plan with foresight into AI's successes and failures, and show analytically that it approximately tracks the impact of optimal AI deployment."
where_b: 4_implications.tex:202: "Notably, this AI strategy isn't necessarily optimal even with the benefit of foresight: a long AI chain with a good probability of success might be optimal even if the prophet knows that it will fail on the first attempt."
why: The intro attaches the word "optimal" to the foresight plan whose cost defines FI; Section 4.2 states explicitly that this plan is sub-optimal even among foresight plans, and gives the reason (a chain worth running despite a known first-attempt failure). If FI were the value of an optimal-with-foresight plan it would be a lower bound on OPT, whereas Proposition \ref{prop:fragmentation} and Lemma \ref{lem:FI.upper.bound} allow $FI$ up to $\tfrac54 OPT$ and Example \ref{ex:FI.tight} attains it ($FI=5/2$ against $OPT=2$, recomputed and confirmed). So the intro's characterization is inconsistent with the proposition itself, not only with the Section 4.2 caveat.
fix: The intro is the wrong side. Drop "optimal": e.g. "the expected cost of a natural execution plan built with foresight into AI's successes and failures."

title: Section 7 states the model requires an AI chain to begin with an automated task; Definition 4 requires no such thing (a length-one chain begins with an augmented step)

where_b: 3_shortrun.tex:89 (Definition \ref{def:ai_chain}): "An AI chain is a contiguous block of one or more sequential steps executed by AI, in which all steps but the final one are automated and the final step is augmented." An AI-augmented step is thus an AI chain of length one, a convention we adopt throughout the paper."
why: Definition 4 constrains the chain's *end* (the last step must be augmented, all earlier ones automated); it places no requirement on the first step, and a length-one chain explicitly begins with an augmented step. The paper states the requirement correctly twice elsewhere — 7_empirics.tex:36 ("requires every automated step to be followed by another automated or augmented step") and 7_empirics.tex:27 ("an automated task followed by a manual one, which the model's definition of a chain does not allow") — so line 143 contradicts both Definition 4 and the paper's own two other renderings of it.
fix: 7_empirics.tex:143 is the wrong side. Replace "that a chain begin with an automated task" with the requirement Definition 4 actually imposes, e.g. "that every automated task be followed by another AI-executed task, with the chain terminating in an augmented one."

title: In the proof of the 5/4 upper bound the maximizing point is written with the wrong sign in the exponent, giving a value $\alpha^{-d(T_j)}=1/2$ that is impossible
where_a: A_omitted_proofs.tex:235: "The ratio between this expression and $\alpha^{-d(T_j)}$ is maximized at $\alpha^{-d(T_j)} = 1/2$, achieving a value of $5/4$ as claimed."
where_b: A_omitted_proofs.tex:234: "$1 + \sum_{s_i \in T_j}(1-\alpha^{d_i})(1+\alpha^{-d_i}) \leq 1 + (1-\alpha^{d(T_j)})(1+\alpha^{-d(T_j)}) = 1 + \alpha^{-d(T_j)} - \alpha^{d(T_j)}$"; and Example \ref{ex:FI.tight} (A_omitted_proofs.tex:242-247), whose tight instance has chain success probability $q_1q_2q_3 = 1/2$, i.e. $\alpha^{d(T)} = 1/2$
why: Write $u = \alpha^{-d(T_j)}$. The ratio is $(1 + u - 1/u)/u = 1/u + 1 - 1/u^2$, whose derivative $-1/u^2 + 2/u^3$ vanishes at $u = 2$, giving $1/2 + 1 - 1/4 = 5/4$. So the maximum is at $\alpha^{-d(T_j)} = 2$, equivalently $\alpha^{d(T_j)} = 1/2$. The value printed, $\alpha^{-d(T_j)} = 1/2$, is not attainable at all: $\alpha \in (0,1]$ and $d \ge 0$ force $\alpha^{-d(T_j)} \ge 1$. The paper's own tightness example confirms the correct point: its optimal chain succeeds with probability $1/2 = \alpha^{d(T)}$, and I recomputed $FI = \tfrac12(1) + \tfrac12(1+2+1) = 5/2$ against $OPT = 1/(1\cdot\tfrac12\cdot 1) = 2$, ratio exactly $5/4$.
fix: Line 235 is the wrong side. Write "maximized at $\alpha^{d(T_j)} = 1/2$" (equivalently $\alpha^{-d(T_j)} = 2$).

title: Appendix H claims no branch of five or more steps reaches τ = +1; Figure OA-18 shows a substantial five-step block in the τ = +1 bin
where_a: writeup/draft_mert/H_external_validation.tex:173 — "Figure~\ref{fig:apqc_tau_by_size} decomposes the distribution by branch length and shows the consequence directly: the mass at $\tau = -1$ consists entirely of three- and four-step branches, and so does most of the spike at $\tau = +1$, where $56\%$ of three-step branches sit against none of the branches with five steps or more."
where_b: The figure that sentence cites, Figure OA-18 panel (a) (`fig:apqc_tau_size_main`), included at writeup/draft_mert/H_external_validation.tex:135 as `plots/apqc_pcf_ordering/tau_distribution_by_size_main_share.png`. Its rightmost bar (τ ∈ [0.9, 1.0], total ≈26.6% of branches) is stacked with all five length groups: ≈10.2% "3 steps", ≈8.1% "4 steps", ≈5.2% "5 steps", ≈2.1% "6-7 steps", ≈1.0% "8+ steps" (legend order light→dark = 3, 4, 5, 6-7, 8+, verified against the legend swatch colors).
why: The histogram spans exactly [−1, 1] in 20 bins of width 0.1, so the rightmost bin is [0.9, 1.0]. For a five-step branch Kendall's τ can only take the values 1, 0.8, 0.6, …, so every five-step branch in that bin has τ = exactly +1. Scaling by the figure's own calibration (n = 63+74+70+75+63 = 345; the "3 steps" segment of that bar is 10.2% ≈ 35 branches = 35/63 = 56%, which is the very number the sentence quotes), the "5 steps" segment of ≈5.2% is ≈18 branches — roughly 26% of the 70 five-step branches — sitting at τ = +1, not "none". fix: The figure is the primary evidence and the 56% figure quoted in the same clause is confirmed by it, so the prose is the wrong side. title: The cost of one inversion in Kendall's τ on a ten-step branch is stated as 0.02; under the paper's own τ normalization it is 0.044
where_a: writeup/draft_mert/H_external_validation.tex:172 — "whereas on a ten-step branch the same inversion costs $0.02$ and leaves $\tau$ near $+1$"
where_b: writeup/draft_mert/H_external_validation.tex:172 — "on a three-step branch it can only take the values $\{-1, -1/3, +1/3, +1\}$"
why: The enumerated three-step value set pins down the normalization the paper is using: τ = 1 − 4d/(n(n−1)) where d is the number of discordant pairs, since for n = 3 this gives {1, 1/3, −1/3, −1} for d = 0,1,2,3, exactly the set quoted. Applying the same formula at n = 10 (45 pairs): one discordant pair gives τ = 1 − 4/90 = 43/45 = 0.9556, a cost of 0.0444, not 0.02. The value 0.02 is 1/45, i.e. the pair's share of the pair count rather than its effect on τ, which is twice that.
fix: Replace "costs $0.02$" with "costs about $0.04$" (τ falls from +1 to 43/45 ≈ 0.96). The qualitative point — that the same inversion barely moves τ on a long branch — is unaffected.

title: "A single inverted pair already registers as a large negative number" on a three-step branch contradicts the τ values listed in the same sentence
where_a: writeup/draft_mert/H_external_validation.tex:172 — "so a single inverted pair already registers as a large negative number"
where_b: writeup/draft_mert/H_external_validation.tex:172 — "on a three-step branch it can only take the values $\{-1, -1/3, +1/3, +1\}$"
why: Under the normalization implied by the quoted value set (τ = 1 − 4d/3 for n = 3), the four values correspond to d = 0, 1, 2, 3 discordant pairs, i.e. τ = +1, +1/3, −1/3, −1. A single inverted pair therefore gives τ = +1/3, which is positive; reaching a negative τ on a three-step branch requires at least two of the three pairs to be inverted. The clause is meant to contrast with "on a ten-step branch the same inversion … leaves τ near +1", but on a three-step branch that same single inversion leaves τ at +1/3, not at a large negative value.
fix: Rewrite as "so a single inverted pair already drags τ from +1 down to +1/3, and two inverted pairs make it negative", which preserves the coarseness point without contradicting the enumerated values.
